title: Quirky, relatable, misleading: ADHD's viral Identity on TikTok
screen_reason: Content analysis of the top 98 TikTok videos returned for #adhd, independently coded by two clinicians against the AWMF S3 ADHD practice guideline. Reports the share of videos rated misleading (87/98 = 89%) and counts for four types of misleading content. That is a quantitative share of items with a denominator, judged against a stated external ground truth, so it meets the CONTENT criterion.

estimates.value_raw: Among the 98 videos analyzed, 87 (89%) were rated as misleading

estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if the two rating clinicians judged it contained content likely to lead viewers to believe inaccurate or unsupported claims about ADHD - not only entirely false statements, but also true-but-non-specific (transdiagnostic) symptoms presented as ADHD-specific, dramatised overexaggeration, and unsubstantiated advice - assessed against the AWMF S3 ADHD guideline

estimates.ground_truth_detail: One clinical psychologist (MN) and one psychiatric resident (MR), both with clinical experience diagnosing and treating ADHD, coded independently; disagreements (4 on the misleading variable) resolved by a third psychologist/senior researcher providing an independent blind rating. Cohen's kappa for misleading content = 0.883. Accuracy benchmark: the interdisciplinary, evidence- and consensus-based S3 practice guideline on ADHD published by the AWMF (2018).
estimates.moderator_quote: On January 3, 2024, a search query for "#adhd" was conducted on the TikTok mobile application (Fig. 1). To prevent any bias from personalized content algorithms influencing the results, the search was done with a newly created account and a newly created email address on a device set to default settings. [...] The first 100 videos appearing under this hashtag were included in the raw dataset
estimates.notes: Construct call for an adjudicator: coded CONTENT, not QUALITY, because items are explicitly coded false/misleading against a stated external ground truth (the AWMF S3 ADHD guideline) by clinicians - there is no DISCERN/GQS/JAMA-style quality instrument here. borderline=true because the 'misleading' label is broad in a way that can catch factually correct material: 28 of the 87 misleading videos were coded for 'transdiagnostic symptoms' that the authors themselves describe as 'generally correct but not specific for ADHD', and 16 for 'overexaggeration'. The implicit claim being judged false is that these behaviours are ADHD-specific, which is why I retained CONTENT with breadth=misleading rather than QUALITY. A stricter, falsity-only variant is given as the second row. Sample is a rank-truncated hashtag feed (the first 100 videos surfaced by TikTok's algorithm to a fresh account), hence denom_selection=curated; the authors stress these are the most-engaged videos, so the 89% is a share of highly visible ADHD content, not of ADHD content on TikTok generally. Unit is the video, not the claim: the authors warn 'findings must not be read as claim-level error rates'. Quote trimmed to the single verbatim print line; the word 'misleading.' that completes the sentence falls on a later line because the .txt rendering interleaves the results column with a table of example videos.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two clinician raters and third-rater adjudication as the main row (Cohen's kappa 0.883 for the misleading judgement); the four misleading subtypes were derived inductively by MN and MR watching all misleading videos together and refining categories iteratively, so no separate reliability statistic is reported for the subtype coding. Benchmark: AWMF S3 ADHD guideline (2018).
estimates.moderator_quote: This process led to the development of four distinct categories of misleading content: (1) factually wrong information, (2) transdiagnostic symptoms, (3) overexaggeration, and (4) unsubstantiated claims.
estimates.notes: Stricter-veracity variant of the 89% row (same 98-video denominator, hence definition_variant=true and within_misinfo_content=false; both counts, 31 and 98, are verbatim, so this is an exact part/whole share under R8, not a computed complement). Confidence medium for one reason an adjudicator should see: the four subtype counts do not reconcile with the misleading total - 31 + 28 + 16 + 13 = 88, plus 'One misleading video did not fit into any of these categories' = 89, against 87 videos rated misleading. Either two videos carry more than one subtype (the text's 'in contrast'/'another' phrasing implies exclusivity) or there is an arithmetic slip in the paper. This does not affect the numerator 31 read as 'videos containing factually wrong information', but it does mean the subtypes should not be treated as a clean partition. The subtype coding was inductive and reported without its own reliability statistic. Quote is the next verbatim print-line fragment of the same sentence ('misleading. Of these videos, 31 were classified as con-'); the denominator (98 videos) is carried by the row above.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The three other misleading subtypes (transdiagnostic symptoms n = 28, overexaggeration n = 16, unsubstantiated claims n = 13) were not entered as rows. They are not veracity-strictness variants that this review can use as prevalence (they are types of misleadingness, two of which the authors say can be factually correct), and their counts do not reconcile with the 87 total (see the second row's notes). Only the strict-falsity subtype was kept, as it is the one that maps onto a narrower breadth code. (2) The HCP subgroup: 'Within the HCP group, misleading content was found in videos by two chiropractors, one optometrist, and one psychotherapist, while the psychiatrist's video stood alone in providing accurate information' - i.e. 4 of the 5 HCP videos were misleading. Not entered: it is a creator-type subgroup, not the paper's headline, and n = 5 is too small to be usable. (3) Figures the paper cites from other studies were NOT extracted (R8): Yeung et al. (21% useful, 52% misleading of the top 100 #ADHD TikToks), Verma & Sinha (92% of 50 #adhdtest videos misleading by an ASRS-screener-coverage rule), Karasavva et al. ('more than half' inconsistent with DSM-5), Leveille (n = 29; 59% humor, 48% self-deprecating humor), Beatty et al. (44% of ADHD questions answered correctly in a US survey, n = 1,025), and the summary range '51% to 92%'. (4) Non-misinformation descriptive shares not extracted because they measure style or authorship rather than veracity: 69% humor, 58% ADHD-deprecating humor (84% of humorous videos), 66% acting/performance, 16% medicalization, 95% non-HCP vs 5% HCP uploads, and the HCP/non-HCP contrasts (0% vs 73% humor, 0% vs 70% performance). (5) Engagement metrics (mean 4,411,437 views etc.) are not prevalence.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of a rank-truncated hashtag sample. Frame: on 3 January 2024 the first 100 videos shown under #adhd on the TikTok mobile app to a newly created account with a new email on a default-settings device (to avoid personalisation); exclusions for no audio/text, languages other than English or German, non-ADHD content, and duplicates removed 2 videos, leaving 98. No response rate applies. Coding: a clinical psychologist and a psychiatric resident, both experienced in ADHD, coded independently for misleading content, humor, ADHD-deprecating humor and medicalization, with all categories applied independently of one another; the lead researcher alone coded HCP status and performance. Disagreements were resolved by a third psychologist/senior researcher giving an independent blind rating. Reliability (Cohen's kappa): misleading 0.883 (4 disagreements), humor 0.853 (6), ADHD-deprecating humor 0.743 (12), medicalization 0.819 (5). Accuracy benchmark: AWMF (2018) S3 ADHD guideline. Misleading subtypes were derived inductively by joint viewing and discussion, with no separate reliability statistic. Author-acknowledged limitations: tiny fraction of TikTok content; video-level (not claim-level) unit; no coding of point-of-view disclaimers or creator self-disclosures; hashtag search differs from the algorithmically personalised feed users actually see.
